claims.text: Pre-exposure Q235 steel has a naturally formed thin native iron-oxide film.
At room temperature, the native oxide film on Q235 steel is compact and protective.
The compact native oxide film resists chloride ingress.
Resistance to chloride ingress slows corrosion of Q235 steel.
Elevated temperature alters the kinetics of oxide formation on Q235 steel in a chloride-containing environment.
The altered oxide-formation kinetics at elevated temperature produce a more porous and defective oxide layer.
A more porous and defective oxide layer provides less protection to the underlying steel.
Loss of oxide-film protection accelerates pit initiation and corrosion.
Under otherwise identical chloride exposure, specimens held near 25°C will lose less weight than specimens held near 60°C.
Under otherwise identical chloride exposure, specimens held near 25°C will develop shallower pits than specimens held near 60°C.
The oxide layer after chloride exposure near 25°C will be more compact than the oxide layer after exposure near 60°C.
Humidity variations may influence oxide-film formation and protective performance.
Additional corrosive species may influence oxide-film formation and protective performance.
The proposed study compares chloride exposure near 25°C and 60°C for approximately 100 hours while holding chloride concentration and humidity constant.
Samples receiving no chloride exposure serve as untreated controls.
